content: The thymus and bone marrow are responsible for presenting developing lymphocytes with self-antigens produced throughout the body. This process eliminates cells that recognize self-antigens, thereby preventing autoimmunity. Hypersensitivity refers to an immune response that causes damage to the body’s own tissues. It is classified into four types (Type I–IV) based on the mechanisms involved and the timing of the reaction. Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate or anaphylactic reaction, often associated with allergies. Symptoms can range from mild discomfort to life-threatening conditions. This reaction is mediated by IgE antibodies released from mast cells and basophils. Type II hypersensitivity occurs when antibodies bind to antigens on the patient’s own cells, marking them for destruction. This is also known as antibody-dependent or cytotoxic hypersensitivity and is mediated by IgG and IgM antibodies. Type III hypersensitivity involves immune complexes, which are aggregates of antigens, complement proteins, and IgG or IgM antibodies. These complexes deposit in various tissues, triggering inflammatory reactions. Type IV hypersensitivity, also called cell-mediated or delayed-type hypersensitivity, typically develops over two to three days. It is involved in many autoimmune and infectious diseases and can also manifest as contact dermatitis, such as poison ivy reactions. These responses are mediated by T cells, monocytes, and macrophages. The adaptive immune system likely evolved with the first vertebrates, as invertebrates do not produce lymphocytes or antibody-based humoral responses. However, many invertebrates utilize mechanisms that appear to be precursors to vertebrate immunity. Even the simplest life forms, such as bacteria, have immune-like systems. Bacteria use a defense mechanism called the restriction modification system to protect themselves from viral pathogens like bacteriophages. Pattern recognition receptors are proteins used by nearly all organisms to identify molecules associated with pathogens. Antimicrobial peptides, such as defensins, are evolutionarily conserved components of the innate immune response found in all animals and plants. In invertebrates, defensins represent the primary form of systemic immunity. The complement system and phagocytic cells are also utilized by most invertebrates. Ribonucleases and the RNA interference pathway, conserved across all eukaryotes, play a role in the immune response to viruses. Unlike animals, plants lack phagocytic cells. Most plant immune responses involve systemic chemical signals that are transmitted throughout the plant. When a part of a plant becomes infected, it produces a localized hypersensitive response, where cells at the infection site undergo rapid apoptosis to prevent the spread of the disease. Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) is a defensive response in plants that renders the entire plant resistant to a specific infectious agent. RNA silencing mechanisms are particularly important in this systemic response, as they can block viral replication. The immune system also plays a critical role in identifying and eliminating tumors. Tumor cells express antigens that are not found on normal cells, making them appear foreign to the immune system. This triggers immune cells to attack the tumor cells. Tumor antigens can originate from various sources. Some are derived from oncogenic viruses, such as human papillomavirus (HPV), which causes cervical cancer. Others are the organism’s own proteins that are normally expressed at low levels but are overexpressed in tumor cells. For example, the enzyme tyrosinase, when overexpressed, can transform melanocytes into melanoma cells. Additionally, mutations in proteins that regulate cell growth and survival can produce cancer-inducing molecules called oncogenes. The primary immune response to tumors involves the destruction of abnormal cells by killer T cells, often with the assistance of helper T cells. Tumor antigens are presented on MHC class I molecules, allowing killer T cells to recognize and target the tumor cells. Natural killer (NK) cells also play a role, particularly when tumor cells have reduced MHC class I expression, a common feature of many tumors. In some cases, antibodies are generated against tumor cells, enabling their destruction via the complement system. However, some tumors evade the immune system and progress to cancer. Tumor cells often reduce the number of MHC class I molecules on their surface, avoiding detection by killer T cells. Additionally, some tumor cells release products that inhibit the immune response, such as the cytokine TGF-β, which suppresses macrophage and lymphocyte activity. Immunological tolerance may also develop against tumor antigens, preventing the immune system from attacking the tumor cells. Paradoxically, macrophages can promote tumor growth when attracted by tumor-released cytokines. These macrophages produce cytokines and growth factors that support tumor development. Furthermore, hypoxia within the tumor and macrophage-derived cytokines can induce tumor cells to decrease production of proteins that block metastasis, thereby facilitating the spread of cancer cells. Hormones can act as immunomodulators, altering the sensitivity of the immune system. For instance, female sex hormones are known to stimulate both adaptive and innate immune responses. This may explain why autoimmune diseases like lupus erythematosus preferentially affect women, often coinciding with puberty. In contrast, male sex hormones like testosterone appear to suppress immune activity. Other hormones, such as prolactin, growth hormone, and vitamin D, also regulate the immune system. A decline in hormone levels with age is thought to contribute to weakened immune responses in older individuals. Conversely, the immune system can regulate certain hormones, such as thyroid hormone activity. The immune system is enhanced by sleep and rest but impaired by stress. Diet also influences immune function; for example, fresh fruits, vegetables, and foods rich in certain fatty acids promote a healthy immune system. Fetal undernourishment can cause lifelong impairments in immune function. In traditional medicine, certain herbs are believed to stimulate the immune system, including echinacea, licorice, ginseng, astragalus, sage, garlic, elderberry, shiitake and lingzhi mushrooms, and hyssop, as well as honey. Studies suggest that these herbs can indeed enhance immune function, although their mechanisms of action are complex and not fully understood. The immune response can be manipulated in medicine to suppress unwanted reactions, such as those caused by autoimmunity, allergies, and transplant rejection, or to stimulate protective responses against pathogens that evade the immune system. Immunosuppressive drugs are used to control autoimmune disorders, reduce inflammation, and prevent organ transplant rejection. Anti-inflammatory drugs are commonly employed to manage the effects of inflammation.
